# Preface: How to Use This Book {.unnumbered epub:type=preface}



Change one number in a dataset, and how many documents are now wrong? If the number was
copied by hand into a report, a slide, an email and a web page, nobody knows without
searching. This book teaches a way of publishing with nothing to search for: you write once,
in plain text, and a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog
and a dashboard all rebuild from that one source with one command. The program that rebuilds
them is Quarto.

## Prompt, Check, Publish {.unnumbered #prompt-check-publish}

The title names the method, a loop you run at every step of both projects. You **prompt** a
*coding assistant*, a program that writes files and runs commands at your request, describing
one small piece of work with its files and columns named. You **check** what it did: read
what changed, look at the result, compare it with the data. An assistant can be fluent, fast
and wrong, so this step is never skipped, and it is always yours. Then Quarto **publishes**,
rebuilding every output from the checked source the same way every time. Chapter 1 explains
why the last step can be trusted, and Chapter 2 how to make the first two reliable.

Every hands-on step in Parts II and III goes once round the loop in @fig-loop.

![Prompt, Check, Publish: the loop this book teaches, with who acts at each step.](media/diagrams/loop){#fig-loop .on-light fig-alt="The loop. Prompt: you ask a coding assistant for one small step, naming the files and ending with a check; Chapter 2. The assistant does the work: it writes files and runs commands. Check: you read what changed, open the result and compare it with the data; Chapter 2. If it is not right, you fix the prompt and go round again. The checked source goes to Publish: Quarto's quarto render rebuilds every output, the same way every time; Chapter 1. Then the next step begins with a new prompt. Small steps, each one checked, every output rebuilt from one source."}

## Who this book is for {.unnumbered}

I wrote this book for researchers, software practitioners, data experts and students: anyone who
works with data/code and needs to share the results. It shows how to publish from one source of
plain-text file (prose & code), using Quarto. Quarto is free and open source traditional
software, so every report, slide deck and web page is reproducible, interactive and of
publication quality. With a coding assistant, work that once took days now takes minutes. Along
the way, I explain the concepts, arguments and decisions behind each step.

You may be new to Quarto, to coding assistants or to both. No programming is assumed: I explain
the Python the assistant writes, but you do not have to write it. If the terminal is
new to you, Chapter 3 teaches the little you need, one checked step at a time.

You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free
GitHub account, and an account with one coding assistant (@sec-before-setup lists what each
needs).

## The two running examples {.unnumbered}

Every concept is tied to one of two projects, both built on real, cited data.

**A London visitor guide** (Part II). For the city's tourism office, you write one guide that
becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and
a published website. Every visitor number in it, from the 7\,116\,929 visits to the
Natural History Museum \(South Kensington\) in 2025 down, is computed from the counts published by
the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions.

**Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities** (Part III). You group Colombia's
municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, from 2016
to 2023, compare health and education outcomes between the kinds, and
publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all from one analysis
script. Most of the data are Colombian open data, joined by official municipality codes;
rainfall comes from the Climate Hazards Center's CHIRPS data and altitude from NASA's SRTM
elevation data (@sec-sources).

## How the book is organised {.unnumbered}

**Part I** covers what you need first: what Quarto does (@sec-quarto), how to work with a
coding assistant safely (@sec-assistant) and how to set up your computer (@sec-setup). The
GitHub account it asks for is free; an assistant's account may not be. Claude Code, for one,
needs a paid plan or pay-per-use billing (checked 2026-11-03; @sec-before-setup lists what
each assistant needs). **Parts II and III** build the two projects, with the statistics
explained on the way, and each ends by changing an input and explaining what the rebuild
changed. The appendices hold the Windows setup, a cheatsheet, troubleshooting, every
checkpoint, the data sources and how this book is built.

By the end of the book you will be able to:

- explain how Quarto turns one source into many formats, and why every rebuild gives the same
  result;
- direct a coding assistant safely: a folder of its own, written rules, and one step per
  prompt, each ending in a check;
- build and publish both projects, the London guide and the water-risk website, each in
  several formats;
- predict which outputs a changed input will update, and check that the rebuild did exactly
  that.

## What a hands-on step looks like {.unnumbered #how-the-hands-on-parts-work}

Each step is a three-part box, explained in @sec-boxes: the exact prompt to give your
assistant, what it will probably run, and the few things only you can do. Prompts are
examples, not transcripts: assistants vary, so check the result rather than the wording. Five
kinds of aside step out of the main text; here is one of each.

::: why
A number computed from the data cannot disagree with the data. Asides like this one explain
the mechanism behind a step, so that you can adapt it to your own project.
:::

::: pitfall
A render started while a live preview is rendering the same file collides with it. Asides
like this one describe failures seen in practice, and how to avoid them.
:::

::: practice
Ask for one step per prompt: a small change is quick to check, and when something breaks you
know which step broke it. Asides like this one hold judgement calls and habits.
:::

::: think
The assistant reports a render with no errors. Is the work checked?

Not yet: a clean render proves that the code ran, not that its numbers are right. Asides like
this one ask a question to answer before you read on; the answer follows it.
:::

::: tryit
Asides like this one are exercises. Think of one document you produce more than once, and
note where each of its numbers comes from.

::: done
you can say which of its numbers are typed by hand and which come from a file.
:::
:::

Steps marked *optional* are for readers who are ahead; nothing later depends on them.

## Two ways through {.unnumbered}

**Self-paced.** Read in order. Chapters 2 and 3 can be read and done in one sitting before
Part II; each chapter of Parts II and III ends at a checkpoint or at the finished example,
where you can stop and resume later.

**Workshop-paced.** The book grew out of a six-hour workshop and keeps its shape, while
explaining what the workshop only had time to show: why each step works, where it fails, and
when not to take it. @sec-workshop has the day's agenda and the chapters each block covers
(@tbl-agenda and @tbl-agenda-water).

## When you get stuck {.unnumbered #when-you-fall-behind}

You will get stuck: an install fails, a prompt goes wrong, a render stops with an error you
have never seen. That is expected, and the book is built for it. Every hands-on block ends at
a *checkpoint*, a folder in the workshop's repository (`checkpoints/`), the copy of the
workshop's files you download during setup (@sec-step-check). It holds the project as it
should be at that point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. The rule is simple:
**stuck for two minutes, catch up**. Where the book reaches a checkpoint, a catch-up box gives
the one line to paste into your assistant (@fig-catch-up).

![Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.](media/diagrams/catch-up){#fig-catch-up .on-light fig-alt="Stuck for two minutes, you paste the line Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/NN/README.md into the assistant. It follows four steps. One, back up your project folder, all but its .venv environment, to a new time-stamped folder beside it. Two, copy the checkpoint in, and for the water project the data if they are missing. Three, render and check a named output. Four, carry on reading from the catch-up box: the project now matches the book at that point."}

The README's last step names the workshop slide to rejoin at. In the book, that place is the
catch-up box itself, so after catching up you carry on reading from the box. If you were stuck
partway through a block, go straight to its box: the checkpoint already holds the steps between
where you stopped and the box. @sec-checkpoints lists every checkpoint.

## Two editions {.unnumbered #two-editions}

This book comes as an e-book (EPUB) and as a website, built from the same source: it is its
own first example of the method. The [website edition](https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/book/)
runs everything interactive: the 3-D scenes of the London map, the k-means steps, the
clusters and Colombia's relief, and two data explorers. The e-book shows each as an animation
or a still, with a link to the live version (the first, the London map, also has a QR code).
Readers that cannot play animations show the first frame, designed as a useful still, and the
website respects your reduced-motion setting.

## Versions and dates {.unnumbered}

The book was built and checked with Quarto 1.10.20 (with its bundled Typst 0.15), Python 3.12
and uv, in November 2026. Facts that change, such as a model's price, an assistant's screens
or a free hosting plan's limits, carry the date they were checked, as in "(checked
2026-11-06)". Some will have changed by the time you read them; the principles around them
should not have.

Chapter 1 needs nothing installed: start there.
